text: - Received into evidence were a number of documentary exhibits that include a revised Management of Paracetamol Poisoning protocol and other documentation that relates to the tracking of blood test results. In addition, the statement dated 26 July 2021 of Dr Peak Mann Mah who is an endocrinologist and general physician at the NALHN, sets out certain changes and measures that have been implemented in relation to the handover of patients between shifts, the recognition of deteriorating patients, the review of patients with significant ingestion of medications and the education of staff. A joint education session between the LMH ED and Medicine Toxicology had been scheduled to occur in 2020 to discuss matters that became evident from Ms Cook’s death. However, this session had been cancelled due to Covid restrictions and demands on medical staff. If this education session has yet to occur, I would urge that it takes place at the earliest opportunity following the delivery of these findings. Response from SA Health •   NALHN has updated their current organisation wide instruction to include changes recommended by the Coroner and will contribute to a system-wide approach to reviewing Paracetamol Overdose protocols. •   NALHN has planned a Grand Round presentation booked for 9 November 2022, which includes teleconference facilities between sites. This session is to include Paracetamol poisoning, protocol/clinical procedure (referencing NALHN and National Guidelines), tracking and following up of blood results, clinical handover, and escalation of care. •   The Department for Health and Wellbeing (The Department) will work with Local Health Networks (LHNs) to determine a consistent system-wide multi-disciplinary approach to clinical education sessions relating to the safe management of patients presenting with Paracetamol over-dose. 19 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2022-23 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court

– The revised Management of Paracetamol Poisoning protocol alters the protocol as it existed at the time of Ms Cook’s presentation to the LMH in that it expands the concept of ‘unknown’ time of ingestion to encompass an ‘uncertain or unreliable history’ in respect of time of ingestion. Secondly, it speaks of a low threshold for commencing NAC in patients with ingestion of 10 grams of paracetamol or more. However, from what can be seen of the revised protocol, it does not provide any further guidance as to what should take place in the case of an anorexic or bulimic patient who has ingested that quantity. In my view the relevance of anorexia or bulimia and their possible effect on glutathione depletion should be spelt out in the protocol. Further guidance should be included to explain the necessary course of action when such a patient is encountered. I so recommend. I direct this recommendation to the attention of the Chief Executive of SA Health. Response from SA Health •   Metropolitan hospitals adhere to the protocols that exist with their site-specific guidelines, including appropriate treatment of patients presenting with anorexia/ bulimia. The Rural Support Service (RSS) are developing a new guideline for Regional hospitals. •   The Department has recommended LHNs review current Paracetamol Overdose clinical guidelines, local procedures, and protocols to include management of patients presenting with 'unknown time of ingestion', 'uncertain or unreliable history' with respect to time of ingestion and anorexic/bulimic patients presenting with Paracetamol overdose. •   The Department will work with LHNs to determine a consistent system-wide multidisciplinary approach to review Paracetamol Overdose protocols and implement procedure change.

- The revised protocol does not appear to emphasise the importance of blood testing for evidence of liver damage in cases where NAC is not administered. Clearly, such blood testing is necessary in all cases, but it is particularly important in cases where NAC is not given for whatever reason. Illustrating this of course is the fact that in Ms Cook’s case, timely blood testing would have dictated the administration of a NAC infusion notwithstanding that it was not ordered in the first instance. I so recommend. I direct this recommendation to the Chief Executive of SA Health. Response from SA Health •   The Department has recommended LHNs review current clinical guidelines, local procedures, and protocols to emphasize the importance of blood testing for evidence of liver damage in cases where NAG is not administered. •   The Department will work with LHNs to determine a consistent system-wide multidisciplinary approach to review Paracetamol Overdose protocols and implement procedure change.

- In her final submission, Ms Giles of counsel assisting suggested that all local health networks in South Australia should implement a policy whereby any patient with a known or suspected paracetamol overdose must have a blood test to measure blood paracetamol concentration at four hours post admission to a hospital. She suggested that this should take place in addition to blood taken at what is reported to be four hours post ingestion, regardless of the reported ingestion time and the apparent reliability of that information. Ms Giles submits that a mandated blood test at four hours post admission in addition to the bloods taken four hours post believed time of ingestion, would allow for a comparison to be made between the levels and should leave no room for error. It would serve as something of a failsafe measure that might capture cases of paracetamol toxicity in which NAC has not been administered due to an incorrect ingestion time. Mr Ambrose on behalf of the NALHN submitted to the Court that he and his client had no difficulty with this sensible recommendation. I agree with those submissions and recommend accordingly. In my view the implementation of that recommendation should be undertaken more broadly than just within NALHN. It seems to me that it ought to have universal application across all public health networks. I therefore direct this recommendation to the attention of the Chief Executive of SA Health. 20 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2022-23 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court

- Ms Giles also submitted that an appropriate recommendation would be that blood tests for liver function should be mandated at 24 hours post admission in all cases of reported or suspected paracetamol overdose in excess of 10 grams regardless of the reported ingestion time and regardless of whether there has been a need to administer a NAC infusion. On behalf of NALHN, Mr Ambrose also agreed with this submission. I agree with those submissions and recommend accordingly. In my view the implementation of that recommendation should be undertaken more broadly than just within NALHN. It seems to me that it ought to have universal application across all public health networks. I therefore direct this recommendation to the attention of the Chief Executive of SA Health. Response from SA Health The recommendations will be considered, and this SA Health report incorporates the responses of the relevant statewide services. •   The Department has recommended LHNs review current Paracetamol Overdose clinical guidelines, local procedures, and protocols to consider the inclusion of the requirement for blood testing of liver function at 24 hours post admission in all cases of reported or suspected ingestion in excess of 10gms of paracetamol. •   The Department will work with LHNs to determine a consistent system-wide multidisciplinary approach to review Paracetamol Overdose protocols and implement procedure change. Rigney, Amber Rose and Mitchell, Korey Lee (Coroner Schapel)

- I recommend that the Premier of South Australia, the Minister for Child Protection and the Chief Executive of Child Protection cause a review of all coronial and other recommendations relating to child protection in the State of South Australia with a view to the implementation of the same.

- I recommend that a complete review be conducted in relation to all of the statutory obligations contained within the Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017 so as to ensure that practices within the Department align with those statutory obligations. Such a review should consist of an examination of all documented and undocumented internal Departmental procedures so as to ensure that they comply with all statutory obligations contained within child protection legislation. Response of the South Australian Government to Recommendations 1 and 2 •   On 25 May 2022, Ms Kate Alexander was appointed by the Minister for Child Protection to conduct a review pursuant to recommendations 1 and 2. Ms Alexander is an Executive Director of the Office of the Senior Practitioner for the New South Wales Department of Family and Community Services and has extensive knowledge of child protection and vast experience as an expert witness in NSW coronial proceedings and Royal Commission hearings. Ms Alexander was appointed to conduct a review of: •    All coronial and other recommendations relating to child protection in the State of South Australia since 2010 and the implementation of the same. •    All statutory obligations contained within the Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017 and the extent to which practices in the Department for Child Protection, and other State Government agencies as may be appropriate, align with those statutory obligations. •   With respect to recommendation 1, the terms of reference of Ms Alexander’s review also required consideration of the most appropriate lead agency(s) for the ongoing implementation of coronial and other recommendations. Ms Alexander’ report has been completed.

- I recommend that on completion of such review, an assessment be made to ensure that the carrying out of all statutory obligations under the Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017 are fully resourced to enable those duties and obligations to be carried out without exception. 21 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2022-23 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court Response of the South Australian Government •   The Government is committed to ensuring adequate resourcing is available to ensure all statutory obligations under the Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017 can be met and will undertake the assessment as recommended. Ms Alexander’s review and report supported that assessment. Pursuant to section 169 of the Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017, a review of the operation of the Act commenced in September 2022, and is being informed by an ongoing community consultation process. This provides an opportunity to support the review of the statutory obligations identified in recommendation 2.

- I recommend that the Chief Executive of Child Protection remind all staff of the Department of the need, especially where there are allegations involving abuse of an illicit drug placing a child at risk, to consider whether in the circumstances police powers in their capacity as child protection officers pursuant to the provisions of the Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017 should be utilised to assist in any assessment or investigation pursuant to that Act. Response of the South Australian Government •   On 14 July 2022, the Chief Executive of the Department wrote to all Department for Child Protection staff emphasising the need, when planning or conducting a child protection investigation or assessment, for staff to consider whether to request that South Australia Police exercise child protection powers in their capacity as authorised child protection officers under the Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017, particularly where there are allegations that the use of an illicit drug by a parent or care giver is placing a child or young person at risk. The Department’s implementation of its Alcohol and Other Drugs Practice Excellence Strategy ensures that practice guidance in this area is regularly reviewed and updated so that it remains contemporary. Thredgold, Holly Alexandra (Coroner Whittle)

- That the pro-forma document in Sunrise EMRPAS which succeeds the paper document ‘Medical Assessment of Patients with Psychiatric Presentation’ be amended to include provision for recording the answer to a question as to whether a person is or has recently been under treatment by a psychiatrist or psychologist, and provision for recording that that psychiatrist or psychologist has been contacted to obtain relevant collateral information. Response from SA Health The recommendation has been accepted and response incorporates actions by the OCP, in consultation with the LHNs and state-wide services, as detailed: •   The OCP, through the Strategic Mental Health Safety and Quality Committee (SMHQIC), is planning a ‘Barriers to Admission’ working group to address concerns raised in relation to mental health presentations and assessment; in particular, the taking of family and longitudinal histories. •   This item, history of mental health treatment and contacting private practitioners, will be a priority for this group. •   LHNs support this recommendation. A change request will be submitted to the Sunrise EMR Mental Health Clinical Speciality Group.

- That guidelines be prepared and issued ‘For the Care of Persons with Comorbid Mental Illness and Substance Use Disorders in Acute Care Settings’. Consideration may be given to achieving this by amendment of the South Australian Guidelines for ‘Working with the Suicidal Person’. The guidelines should acknowledge and state, in particular, a) that the provision of mental health services is not dependent on sobriety, and is not restricted to situations in which there is a perceived risk of suicide and b) that the presence of alcohol and/or drug intoxication does not preclude early assessment, although it may indicate the need for further 22 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2022-23 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court assessment when the person is no longer intoxicated. When a request for assessment is received, it is not appropriate to insist that the person be free from the effects of alcohol and/or drugs. Response from SA Health The recommendation has been accepted and response incorporates actions by the OCP, in consultation with the LHNs and state-wide services, as detailed: •   It is noted that the South Australian Guidelines for ‘Working with the Suicidal Person’ is a document that requires review. •   The suggestions proposed will be forwarded to both the Towards Zero team and the ‘Barriers to Admission’ working group for their consideration with the intention of updating this document. DASSA will provide assistance with this process. •   The revision will consider NSW Clinical Guidelines: ‘for the Care of Persons with Comorbid Mental Illness and Substance Use Disorders in Acute Care Settings’ document, which includes evidence informed risk assessment tools and screening processes.

- That clinicians practising in hospital emergency departments should assess with a critical mind, a patient’s denials of current suicidal intent and should consider the possibility that denials of important and critical circumstances may be engendered by a desire to be discharged from the hospital. In particular, denials of suicidal ideation should be evaluated against the patient’s documented medical history and collateral history, including collateral history obtained from the persons treating psychiatrist or psychologist. Response from SA Health The recommendation has been accepted and response incorporates actions by the OCP, in consultation with the LHNs and state-wide services, as detailed: •   This is supported by LHNs. It will be followed up through clinical education, and change management (the Towards Zero approach). •   The OCP will continue to provide suicide risk mitigation training (the Connecting with People approach) which includes demographic and social/personal background, clinical factors in history and mental state examination; and suicidal thoughts warning signs. •   This training is available for all clinicians in SA. Recommended ED staff will be encouraged to attend suicide risk mitigation training.

- That the extent of availability at public hospitals of after-hours contact details for private psychiatrists be investigated, with a view to then considering the feasibility of establishing a register of such details. This recommendation is made because the Court heard evidence from Dr Schirripa that on a number of occasions as a private psychiatrist, he has not been contacted about one of his patients who was admitted to a public emergency department. The suggestion was made that private psychiatrists’ after-hours contact details may not be available in emergency departments, but this was not explored in this inquest. Response from SA Health The recommendation has been accepted and response incorporates actions by the OCP, in consultation with the LHNs and state-wide services, as detailed: •   The OCP will work with the LHNs to facilitate contact by public services with private psychiatrists if a consumer of theirs presents to the ED to discuss treatment options (see response to recommendation 1). •   It is noted that private psychiatrists do make arrangements with public mental health services to assist with consumers at risk when they are on leave. 23 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2022-23 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court •   The Chief Psychiatrist will raise this issue with the Chair of SA Branch RANZCP, and the local branch committee, to encourage private psychiatrists to consider providing their contact details to EDs if they have concerns about any of their consumers and to discuss the best approach to a contact register. •   Access to private psychiatrists is supported by the LHNs. Weekes, Virginia Anne & Files, Craig Malcolm (Coroner White)

- SAAS undertake a documented longitudinal clinical review on MPDS determinant 26 CO2 sick person abnormal breathing, to confirm the appropriateness of a Priority 3 response to this type of event. Response from SA Health •   A review of 12 months’ data including overrides and upgrades, and changes to assigned priority was conducted. This review determined if change was required to the response priority by the MPDS Review Workgroup. •   The MPDS Review Workgroup recommendation was endorsed by the Clinical Dispatch Review Group. •   The MPDS Review Workgroup recommended that no change occur, and determinant 26 CO2 remains a priority 3.

- SAAS reconsider each of the determinants currently allocated as a Priority 3 response in acknowledgement of the actual average response times recorded in 2020. Response from SA Health •   The MPDS Review Workgroup conducted a review of all high-risk Priority 3 determinants, many of which were based on Richard Larsen’s report that was tendered at the Coronial Inquest, as well as determinants identified within the Safety Learning System (SLS) the Adverse Events Program. •   Additional data analysis of MPDS determinants aligning to this recommendation was also completed. •   This review recommended some alterations to determinant responses, all of which were accepted and endorsed by the Clinical Dispatch Review Group.

- SAAS should reconsider the Tactical Deployment Plan with particular respect to expanding the range of ambulances for dispatch to a 26 CO2. Secondly, SAAS should examine whether the tasking rules need to change in order to achieve more flexibility in times of increased demand. Response from SA Health •   A review and update of the Tactical Deployment Plan in relation to this case has been completed. This is a fluid document and continues to be reviewed and refined. •   It is appreciated that ambulance services are increasingly extending the role that they play in pre-hospital health provision and the pathways of care that they provide. Not all patients will get a traditional ambulance response and it is important that SAAS offers integrated, flexible care options through early and effective triage of calls for assistance. An expansion of Virtual Care Services, Alternate Care Pathways and ambulance and hospital avoidance strategies have been made available to SAAS clinicians with a view to ensuring resources are available to provide a response to requests for service. •   SAAS has introduced a number of strategies to address periods of increased demand to avoid wherever possible, delayed responses with consideration to some of the external factors contributing to those delays. •   As part of the Surge Management Review, we have introduced strategies within our Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) to support informed patient decision, such as informing the patient or caller if there are any delays, and referral to our clinicians to discuss alternative safe and appropriate travel options, and clinical care pathways. 24 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2022-23 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court

- SAAS review the EOC clinician call-back policy to ensure that a call-back request is submitted to the clinicians with sufficient time to ensure that contact is made before the end of the target response period. Response from SA Health •   A complete review of the Out of Criteria Call-back System (OOCC) has been conducted with a new procedure (PRO-341) developed and approved for use within SAAS. This procedure has been developed to ensure appropriate system oversight of delayed ambulance attendance. •   OOCC are now conducted by Emergency Medical Dispatch Support Officer (EMDSO) using the Medical Priority Dispatch System (MPDS). Timeframes for OOCC are: •     Priority 2 – 30 minutes (un-dispatched primary P2 events) •     Priority 3 – 60 minutes •     Priority 4 – 60 minutes •     Priority 5 – 60 minutes •   Proactive event review and scene contact by a clinician in the EOC can occur sooner where a patient will benefit from review or clinical input.

- SAAS review and provide a documented procedure for the management of call-back requests to provide guidance in relation to the triage of the request queue to determine the most appropriate order of action and, secondly, to ensure that requests remain active and visible on screen until the call-back is definitively actioned. This is consistent with the recommendation made by Richard Larsen. Response from SA Health •   A complete review of the Out of Criteria Call-back System (OOCC) has been conducted with a new procedure (PRO-341) developed and approved for use within SAAS.

- During times of increased demand, SAAS ensures an Emergency Operation Centre clinician assists with dispatch decisions to ensure that those in need receive attention as a matter of priority. Response from SA Health •   PRO-346 Exit Scripting: Care Pathway and Demand Management Procedure defines strategies that can be enacted to support demand, including finding opportunities to reduce the likelihood of a surge, as well as providing opportunity to assist managing demand surges with a Demand Clinician. •   Interim PRO-354 Extreme Demand Dispatch Principles also provides a framework which supports dispatchers decision making to identify those patients at highest risk of deterioration. This includes further stratification via the MPDS alphanumeric code, as well as clinician assessment and/or oversight.

- SAAS ensure that complete addresses are available to be displayed to crew members on all screens within an ambulance where the address is displayed, and on their pagers. Response from SA Health •   A ‘landmark’ field has been added to the Dispatch Alert Screen which pops up when a Unit is tasked to an event. This is in addition to the normal placement of the landmark details on the Dispatch Report. •   This change has been deployed to all Mobile Data Terminals (MDT). •   SAAS have been unable to include the additional detail on pagers. •   Communication to on road crews has included the importance of checking the MDT or accessing the EOC via the Government Ratio Network (GRN) if clarification is required. 25 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2022-23 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court

- SAAS undertake a review of operational escalation and response systems to maintain consistency in service delivery during times of increased triple zero calls, and/or ambulance response demands. Response from SA Health •   The Capacity Management Plan is available to be applied during times of increased service demand or other operational pressure. •   SAAS will undertake a review of this plan.

- SAAS undertake an urgent review of ambulance resourcing within the metropolitan area to identify current and future requirements that will ensure patient safety, consistency of service delivery and that all performance KPIs can be routinely achieved. Response from SA Health •   In alignment with election commitments announced in March 2022, SAAS are undertaking an operational growth plan that includes: •    The recruitment of 350 new Paramedics, Ambulance Officers, and Emergency Operations Centre staff. •    Construction of 5 new SAAS stations, upgrading of 10 stations and the rebuilding of 4 stations. •    Delivery of an additional 36 new ambulances. •    Construction of a new Emergency Operations Centre and State Health Control Centre.

- SAAS review the management of call back requests to ensure that the EOC clinicians are provided optimal systems-based support to ensure that pending call back requests are easily identifiable and are either actioned or called with a reason documented. Response from SA Health •   A complete review of the Out of Criteria Call-back System (OOCC) has been conducted with a new procedure (PRO-341) developed and approved for use within SAAS. •   Development of a dashboard that tracks and measures volume and completion in real time to provide oversight of this activity. Wotton, Jeremy Dane (Coroner Kereru)

- That consideration is given to regular training for Emergency Department staff in the symptoms of posterior circulation stroke. Response from SA Health •   This is supported by LHNs. It will be followed up through clinical education, and change management (the Towards Zero approach).

- That consideration is given to developing a clear pathway for Emergency Department clinicians to follow when symptoms of vertigo or dizziness are both episodic and continuous. Response from SA Health •   This is supported by LHNs. It will be followed up through clinical education, and change management (the Towards Zero approach).

- That consideration is given to engaging the on-call Stroke Unit when the HINTS examination is considered to be indicated in the Emergency Department. Response from SA Health •   This is supported by LHNs. It will be followed up through clinical education, and change management (the Towards Zero approach). 26 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2022-23 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court Response to Recommendations - Deaths In Custody During the year the subject of this report, the following reports detailing any actions taken or proposed to be taken in consequence of recommendations made in the case of a death in custody, were received by the State Coroner: Curran, Michael Anthony (Coroner Schapel) Recommendation - In the inquest into the death of a DCS prisoner, Leonard Edward Dodson, 10 this Court repeated an earlier recommendation that had been made in an inquest into the death of another prisoner Franklin Delano Miller.11 That recommendation was directed to the issue of continuity of care within the prison health system. It was as follows: 'That the Medical Director of the South Australian Prison Health Service assign to a senior medical officer or officers within the Service the responsibility of maintaining oversight of the medical treatment and investigation of those prisoners within institutions operated by the Department for Correctional Services who are suspected of suffering from a serious or life threatening illness, especially in circumstances where the medical treatment and investigation of such prisoners is being conducted by medical practitioners who are not employees of the Service' The Court repeats that recommendation. Response from SA Health •     Mr Curran passed away in 2015.
